clips.text: Check calibration before measuring. At a paper speed of twenty-five millimeters per second, one small horizontal box represents zero point zero four seconds. One large box represents zero point two zero seconds. At the usual gain of ten millimeters per millivolt, one small vertical box represents zero point one millivolt. Different speed or gain changes these relationships. A whole cardiac cycle is not always zero point eight seconds; its duration changes with rate.

clips.text: The P wave represents atrial depolarization. In a typical sinus rhythm in lead two, it is upright and similar from beat to beat. The P R interval runs from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the Q R S complex. A common adult reference is zero point one two to zero point two zero seconds. It includes atrial depolarization and conduction toward the ventricles, including the A V nodal delay. It is not the duration of that delay alone.

clips.text: The Q R S complex represents ventricular depolarization. Measure from its beginning to its end, at the transition into the S T segment called the J point. A duration below zero point one two seconds is usually described as narrow in adult rhythm teaching. Not every complex contains a visible Q, R, and S wave. A wide complex can reflect ventricular origin, but also bundle-branch block, aberrant conduction, pre-excitation, pacing, or other causes.

clips.text: The S T segment extends from the J point to the start of the T wave. The T wave represents ventricular repolarization. Atrial repolarization is usually obscured by the much larger Q R S complex. A U wave may follow the T wave, but is not always visible. S T elevation or depression can have several causes; a single teaching strip does not establish infarction or ischemia without the full clinical and lead context.

clips.text: The Q T interval runs from the start of the Q R S complex to the end of the T wave. It spans ventricular depolarization and repolarization. Q T changes with heart rate, so interpretation often uses a corrected value, called Q T c. The half-R-R rule is only a rough screening shortcut, not a substitute for proper correction and context. Different correction formulas have limitations, especially at very fast or slow rates.

clips.text: Use the same method on every strip. First, assess regularity. Second, calculate atrial and ventricular rates when possible. Third, examine P waves and their relationship to Q R S complexes. Fourth, measure P R intervals and look for patterns. Fifth, measure Q R S duration and compare shapes. Sixth, evaluate Q T where the strip permits it. Describe the evidence before choosing a rhythm name. Electrical rate does not necessarily equal an effective pulse rate.

clips.text: Compare successive R to R intervals for ventricular regularity and P to P intervals for atrial regularity. Calipers or a marked strip can help. An early atrial, junctional, or ventricular beat may interrupt an otherwise regular rhythm. Describe the underlying rhythm and then the premature complex. Ectopic means originating outside the usual pacemaker site; not every ectopic event is premature, because escape beats arise late when higher pacing fails.

clips.text: On a six-second strip, count Q R S complexes and multiply by ten for an estimated ventricular rate. For a regular rhythm at standard speed, divide three hundred by the number of large boxes between consecutive R waves, or fifteen hundred by the small-box count. Three large boxes equal fifteen small boxes, so both calculations give one hundred beats per minute. Eighteen small boxes give about eighty-three. Those are different intervals, not competing answers for the same spacing.

clips.text: If a verified practice strip is available in the website, work through it now. Mark P waves, measure the P R interval, measure Q R S duration, and compare R to R spacing. If atrial activity is not visible, say so rather than inventing a P wave. Record what can and cannot be measured. A strip's label must come from the actual image and measurements; the audiobook's references to unseen numbered figures are not enough to recreate their answers.
